title: Rubio and Lavrov Meet to Discuss Ukraine Conflict and Regional Tensions
text:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov held a high-profile meeting in Manila to explore potential avenues for resolving the Russia-Ukraine conflict and other areas of cooperation. Meanwhile, Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong condemned a recent Chinese missile test as provocative, raising tensions in the region. Rubio also discussed regional issues, including the South China Sea disputes, with Chinese and Indian counterparts.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov in Manila, Philippines on July 23, 2026, on the sidelines of the ASEAN Regional Forum (ARF).
This high-profile meeting aimed to discuss potential avenues for resolving the Russia-Ukraine conflict, among other issues. Rubio acknowledged that U.S. efforts to broker an end to the war had slowed, but expressed openness to renewed talks if the opportunity arose. He emphasized the importance of maintaining a relationship with Russia despite disagreements, citing their status as the two largest nuclear-armed countries. Lavrov, meanwhile, planned to query Rubio about recent statements by U.S. President Donald Trump suggesting a settlement was near.
Beyond Ukraine, the two ministers intended to explore other areas of potential cooperation between the U.S. and Russia during their meeting. Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong also addressed regional concerns during her visit, condemning a recent Chinese missile test as provocative and destabilizing. The test, conducted without adequate notification, raised tensions in the region, particularly given China's rapid military build-up.
Rubio held separate meetings with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar, discussing a range of issues including the South China Sea disputes. The U.S. has long expressed concern about China's activities in the region, which it believes disadvantages smaller claimant countries like the Philippines. Tensions in the South China Sea remain high, with Taiwan and several ASEAN members also involved in territorial standoffs
